chapters.title: The Truth about Relativity
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter uses the Economist subscription decoy and social comparison to show that value is judged against nearby alternatives, not in isolation.
chapters.coreMove: Remove the planted comparison and rebuild the choice around the options that actually compete for your goal.
chapters.commonMisread: Comparison is always bad or envy is the whole lesson.

chapters.title: The Fallacy of Supply and Demand
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter argues that first prices, even arbitrary ones, become anchors that make later prices and demand feel coherent.
chapters.coreMove: Build your own estimate before the first visible number turns into the ruler for every later judgment.
chapters.commonMisread: High prices are always manipulative or negotiation is only about bargaining harder.
mustNotDriftInto: shopping around as the whole fix

chapters.title: The Cost of Zero Cost
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter shows that free offers produce an emotional pull that hides real costs and makes inferior choices feel riskless.
chapters.coreMove: Price the hidden costs of free before the zero overwhelms the better tradeoff.
chapters.commonMisread: Free things are always bad or frugality is the issue.

chapters.title: The Cost of Social Norms
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter distinguishes social norms from market norms and shows how small payments can crowd out goodwill.
chapters.coreMove: Identify the norm in force before introducing money, because a tiny payment can reclassify the whole relationship.
chapters.commonMisread: Pay people more or never pay people for help.

chapters.title: The Influence of Arousal
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter shows that people in calm states mispredict their choices under arousal, anger, attraction, fear, or heat.
chapters.coreMove: Make the safety decision while calm, then remove the option to renegotiate it when the hot state arrives.
chapters.commonMisread: Willpower fails because people are weak or desire is inherently irrational.

chapters.title: The Problem of Procrastination and Self-Control
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter uses deadlines and self-imposed constraints to show that people need externally visible commitments to protect long-term aims.
chapters.coreMove: Turn a distant intention into staged commitments that create consequences before the final deadline.
chapters.commonMisread: Better time management or motivation is enough.

chapters.title: The High Price of Ownership
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter explains the endowment effect, where ownership inflates valuation and makes giving up an object feel like a loss.
chapters.coreMove: Ask what you would pay for the thing today before ownership makes its loss feel larger than its use.
chapters.commonMisread: Sentimental attachment is foolish or selling old things is always rational.

chapters.title: Keeping Doors Open
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter shows that people spend resources preserving options even when those options are unlikely to matter.
chapters.coreMove: Let a low-value option close so attention can move to the choice that actually matters.
chapters.commonMisread: Flexibility is bad or people should specialize in everything.

chapters.title: The Effect of Expectations
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter shows that labels, prior beliefs, and presentation change experienced taste and evaluation before evidence is judged.
chapters.coreMove: Blind the cue that is shaping the experience before deciding what you actually perceive.
chapters.commonMisread: Expectations are placebo magic or branding is always fake.

chapters.title: The Power of Price
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter shows that price can change experienced effectiveness because people use cost as a signal of potency or quality.
chapters.coreMove: Separate the price signal from the result before letting expensive become synonymous with effective.
chapters.commonMisread: Cheap is always as good as expensive or placebo means fake.

chapters.title: The Context of Our Character, Part 1
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter shows that people cheat by small amounts when they can preserve an honest self-image, and that timely moral reminders reduce it.
chapters.coreMove: Move the honesty cue to the moment before rationalization starts.
chapters.commonMisread: People are either honest or dishonest as fixed character types.

chapters.title: The Context of Our Character, Part 2
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter shows that cheating becomes easier when value is represented by tokens, goods, credits, or other noncash forms.
chapters.coreMove: Translate indirect value back into money before moral distance softens the rule.
chapters.commonMisread: This is only about stealing office supplies.

chapters.title: Beer and Free Lunches
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter uses public ordering and preference distortion to show that predictable irrationality creates low-cost design fixes.
chapters.coreMove: Remove the audience or sequence pressure so the real preference can surface cheaply.
chapters.commonMisread: The lesson is only about beer or social conformity.
